title: How to learn something from this book
text: 学习闭环的阅读任务：每一步都要留下可以复查的证据。  0.1 Start with a problem that needs no programming  A ruler lies on a desk. A small object moves from the 12 cm mark to the 19 cm mark. What is its change in position? You probably calculate $19-12=7$ cm. This already contains the basic structure of the book: an observable start, an observable finish, a calculation rule, and a conclusion with a unit.  This small step exposes three questions that recur throughout the book. What object is measured? Which rule and direction convention are used? Can another person reproduce the result? Matrices, derivatives, probability, robot control, and neural networks are more complex, but they must answer the same questions. 0.2 Four learning actions      Prediction matters. Reading an answer after it appears easily creates the illusion that it was already known. A prediction leaves something that can be compared. A wrong prediction is not a failure; it locates the part of the earlier model that needs revision.  0.3 What to do when a word is unfamiliar The main danger in learning from zero is not slowness but pretending to know. The first use of a necessary term includes a Chinese explanation, its standard English name, and an observable example. If it remains unclear, place it in a question sheet instead of replacing it with another unknown term.  0.4 AI can help, but it cannot perform your check AI can re-explain an idea, generate another example, suggest causes of an error, or inspect intermediate derivation steps. Its output is still a candidate answer that needs verification. It may use concepts not yet learned, invent functions, omit units, or produce a fluent but invalid explanation.  0.5 When to continue and when to stop Reading speed is not a completion criterion. Each chapter has an entry and an exit. The entry states the real prerequisites; the exit requires an observable product. If the exit task fails, return to the nearest gap rather than rereading everything or jumping to a more advanced chapter.  0.6 Exercises and answers   合上本书，向一个没有读过本章的人解释四个学习动作，并用“从12 cm到19 cm”的例子演示。若需要照着标题才能说出，就再做一次0.1节的反向移动预测。 建立你的第一张问题表，只写三个当前真正不理解的词。第01章将从“程序是什么、文件在哪里、Python如何运行”开始，不预设任何编程经验。

title: Your first computer-executed calculation
text: 第一次运行程序时要追踪的链条：从路径中的文件到终端中的证据。  1.1 A computer does not understand the problem statement  First make the scene explicit: an object moves from the 12 cm mark to the 19 cm mark. So 12 cm is the start, 19 cm is the finish, and the change is “finish minus start”: $19-12=7$ cm. A computer does not know this automatically. It processes values by explicit instruction and does not know that 19 is the finish, 12 is the start, or that the result is in centimetres. Programming therefore begins by turning omitted human knowledge into explicit steps.  Comparing a program file to an experiment procedure is imperfect but useful at first: the file stores steps, the interpreter executes them, and the terminal issues the command to execute this procedure now. Output produced during a run is not the program file itself. 1.2 File names, extensions, and paths The file name `first_calculation.py` contains the stem `first_calculation` and the extension `.py`. The extension indicates Python source. A path locates the file in nested folders, for example `E:/codex/robotics-study/first_calculation.py`. Different folders can contain files with the same name, so saying “I ran `first_calculation.py`” is not yet precise.  1.3 The first program: predict each line In the program below, `start_cm` stores the start (12 cm) and `finish_cm` stores the finish (19 cm). Therefore “finish minus start” is written as `finish_cm - start_cm` in code.      The first line associates the start, 12 cm, with `start_cm`; the second associates the finish, 19 cm, with `finish_cm`; the third evaluates finish minus start, `finish_cm - start_cm`, and associates the result with `change_cm`; the final line displays the result. Executed top to bottom, the output should be `7`.  1.4 Saving and running the file Save the code as `first_calculation.py`. In PowerShell, enter its folder and run `python first_calculation.py`. The first `python` starts the interpreter; the following file name tells it which program to read. If the terminal is not in the file's folder, change directory first or use the complete path.  The prompt, command, and output have different roles. The prompt shows the working directory; the command is your request; the following 7 is program output. Do not copy all terminal text into the Python file. 1.5 Values, names, operators, and expressions The 12 and 19 are integer values. The minus sign is an operator. `finish_cm - start_cm` is an expression that produces a value when evaluated. Here the equals sign performs assignment: evaluate the right side, then associate the result with the name on the left. It does not assert that both sides are forever equal.  1.6 Why units appear in names Python does not prevent adding centimetres to metres. Including a unit in a simple name, such as `length_cm` or `speed_m_per_s`, is not a complete unit system, but it improves first reading and checking. Names use letters, digits, and underscores and cannot begin with a digit.  1.7 Does the program survive changed input? One correct answer does not prove the rule. Change the start to 19 cm and finish to 12 cm; the prediction is -7. Then set both to 12 cm; the prediction is 0. These inputs check reverse motion and the boundary case of no motion.  1.8 Reading an error for the first time Deliberately change the last line to `print(change_mm)`. The program raises an error because the name `change_mm` was never created. An error is not a judgment of you; it is a record of where execution stopped. Read the final line first for the error type and nearby cause, then inspect the named file and line.    1.9 Put a check inside the program Python's `assert` expresses a condition that must hold here. If the condition is true, execution continues; if false, execution stops and reports the failed check.  The double equals `==` compares two values; the single equals `=` assigns. Deliberately change the expected value to 8 and observe execution stop before printing. An assertion does not prove correctness for every input, but it stores one concrete expectation in the program so later changes can be checked. 1.10 The first complete mini-experiment Now compare three motion cases. We do not yet use loops or functions because those concepts have not been established. Repeating a few lines is inelegant, but it keeps every step visible. Later chapters show how to remove the repetition. 三个可检查的移动案例 / Three checkable motion cases The predicted output is `7 -7 0`. The cases cover an ordinary case, a reversed case, and a boundary case. Text beginning with `#` is a comment: it explains code but is not executed as a Python instruction. 1.11 From ruler to robot without skipping levels The position of a mobile robot on a line, the angle of a robot joint, and the pixel location of a camera target can all begin with final value minus initial value. Their units and meanings differ. At this point, notice only the shared structure; vectors, matrices, and controllers are not yet required. Later chapters add multiple directions and time after one-dimensional change is clear.  1.12 Exercises, answers, and completion standard    合上书，回答：程序文件、Python解释器、终端、命令和输出分别是什么？然后在一个新文件夹中重新完成一次正向、反向和零变化实验。 保存程序、终端命令、预期输出、实际输出和一次错误修复记录。下一章从数值、单位、变量和表达式继续，随后先学习列表、循环和条件，再进入代数、矩阵与 Jacobian，不会直接跳入 NumPy。

title: Numbers, units, variables, and expressions
text: 单位尺度图的阅读任务：先确认对象和尺度，再进行换算。  2.1 A number is not a quantity  The number 7 is only a value. 7 mm, 7 cm, 7 s, and 7 kg describe different kinds of quantities. A quantity contains at least a value and a unit; robot systems often also require an object, direction, frame, and time. We begin by making values and units explicit.   2.2 Unit conversion multiplies by a ratio equal to one Since $1\ \mathrm{m}=1000\ \mathrm{mm}$, the ratio $1\ \mathrm{m}/1000\ \mathrm{mm}$ divides one length by the same length and therefore equals one. Converting 35 mm to metres can be written as  Millimetres cancel between numerator and denominator, leaving metres. This is safer than memorising “divide by 1000,” because a reversed conversion becomes visible in the units. To convert 0.035 m back to millimetres, use the reciprocal ratio.  A round-trip check converts from A to B and back to A, then checks whether the original value is recovered. It does not prove all unit logic, but catches many direction and scale errors. 2.3 Integers and decimal numbers Python uses different types for different kinds of data. `35` is an integer and `0.035` is a floating-point number. Floating-point values approximate real numbers with decimals. Later numerical-computing chapters explain their representation; for now, know that some decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly in binary.  `abs` computes absolute value. The check asks whether the difference is smaller than $10^{-12}$ rather than requiring exact equality. A tolerance must not be chosen arbitrarily large; it should be stricter than the task error allowance and appropriate to the scale. 2.4 Evaluation order in an expression The expression $2+3\times4$ evaluates multiplication first and gives 14, whereas $(2+3)\times4$ gives 20. Python uses the same basic precedence. Even when precedence is known, parentheses should expose the intended structure in unit conversions, averages, and error formulas.   2.5 Variables change with execution order The mathematical equation $x=x+1$ cannot hold for an ordinary real number, because subtraction would give $0=1$. In Python, `x = x + 1` is not an equation: it reads the old value, adds one, and associates `x` with the new value.  This allows a program to record state, but means code cannot be read without execution order. Loops later repeat such updates; robot state, training steps, and experiment counts all use this mechanism. 2.6 A measurement is not an exact truth  Reading 35 mm from a ruler with 1 mm divisions does not imply that the true length is exactly $35.000\ldots$ mm. The reading depends on resolution, viewing angle, placement, and operator. A measurement record should contain at least a value, unit, and measurement condition.  If blade assembly allows 0.02 mm of position error while the measuring tool reliably resolves only 1 mm, adding decimal places does not solve the problem. `35.000000` looks more precise but contains no additional measurement information. 2.7 A minimal measurement program 单位、平均值和容差的最小实验 / Minimal experiment with units, mean, and tolerance The program preserves the unit of three readings, computes their mean, and compares the absolute difference from a target. The Boolean value `within_tolerance` is either `True` or `False`; the next chapter formally introduces comparisons and Booleans. For now, predict the three printed results and compare them with the run.  2.8 Connections across robot scenarios  These cases establish only the shared principle that a value needs semantics. Navigation, torque, and neural networks are not prerequisites here. When each topic is introduced, we return to the same table with additional mathematics and code. 2.9 Exercises, answers, and completion standard   不用看书，解释数值、量、量纲、单位、变量、表达式、误差、不确定性和容差的区别。然后运行2.7节程序，改变一个读数并预测哪些输出会改变。 保存一次包含原始读数、单位、平均值、目标、容差、预测和实际结果的运行记录。下一章将正式建立相等、大小比较、方程、不等式和布尔判断。

title: Scientific Python: turning mathematics into reproducible experiments
text: 运行身份决定结果能否成为证据 / Run identity determines whether a result is evidence 6.1 A list is the smallest dataset A single variable stores one value; a list stores an ordered collection of values. A mobile robot trajectory can use one list for positions and another for joint angles. A list does not yet involve vectors, matrices, or NumPy; it is the smallest container for keeping related data together.  Units remain explicit: every element is a position in centimetres. The container does not know the unit; the person writing the code does. Putting the unit in a name or comment is a convention shared by all later scientific programs. 6.2 Loops: repeat one action over a collection To subtract adjacent positions, do not copy the calculation line by line. A loop visits each adjacent pair and appends the result to a new list. This repetition is the cleaner form deferred in Chapter 01, and we now establish it.  Before running, write a small table showing each $i$, the two accessed positions, and the computed change. A loop does not change the calculation rule; it makes execution order and accessed data explicit.    6.3 Conditions: choose an action at the right time A robot does not always execute the same action. A negative change means motion opposite to the chosen positive direction; zero means no change; otherwise the motion is positive. Use `if/elif/else` to express the branches explicitly.  Conditions also write the simplest input-output relation into the program. The example still uses one-dimensional positions and ordinary Python types rather than NumPy, so every branch can be checked line by line. 6.4 Tests are not a last-minute task Tests turn stated properties into executable assertions. The direction branches must handle forward, backward, and zero change; a centimetre-to-metre conversion must keep units consistent; an empty list must be rejected rather than allowing a loop to silently produce a wrong number. Writing properties first changes debugging from guessing to locating.  This uses only the lists, loops, conditions, and functions already established. Tests for NumPy and matrix properties are added after matrices are actually defined, so untested concepts do not enter the test suite prematurely. 6.5 Randomness, configuration, and logs An uninterpretable experiment is often caused not by algorithmic complexity, but by unrecorded parameters and environment. Save at least the random seed, data version, model parameters, software version, run time, and metrics. Configuration can be stored separately from code, but the textbook keeps it next to the experiment explanation.   6.6 From toy examples to engineering modules Toy examples isolate one concept; engineering modules handle real inputs. They should not be confused. A toy example should be short, transparent, and hand-checkable. An engineering module needs interfaces, error handling, tests, and logs. The textbook embeds the short code beside the idea, then provides a reusable module at the chapter exit. 6.7 Numeric precision comes later; first establish a checkable record From the second half of this chapter, NumPy arrays hold collections of values. They resemble the earlier lists, but an array carries an explicit shape and numeric type, which makes bulk computation faster. Treat it as a shaped numeric list for now; vectors and matrices are defined formally in the following chapters, where broadcasting, conditioning, and linear-algebra properties become required reading. Floating-point values are not real numbers. Millimeter calibration errors, visual probabilities, matrix condition numbers, and deep-network gradients live at different scales. float32 is often enough for control prototypes; float64 is useful for small geometric calibration and numerical checks. Mixed precision can accelerate training but requires overflow, underflow, and loss-scaling checks.  Do not use `np.linalg.inv` for every linear system; prefer `solve`, QR, or SVD and record the condition number. Use log-sum-exp for probabilities instead of exponentiating first. Add an explicit $\epsilon$ to normalization and log its value and effect.  6.8 Data schemas: make each record carry physical semantics CSV fits simple tables, but robot trajectories need nested metadata, variable lengths, and binary images. Whether using JSONL, Parquet, or a database, each record needs episode id, sequence index, timestamp, frame, units, sensor source, and status. Schema changes need versions; migrations should be explicit rather than guessed.  Dataset traceability: arrays need provenance A NumPy array stores values, not which episode, frame, workpiece, or time produced them. Before sending an array to a model, write provenance into the record; otherwise identical shapes may come from training, validation, or future observations while the code remains superficially correct.   6.9 Plots and uncertainty: a figure is not evidence by itself Plots discover patterns and anomalies; they should not hide uncertainty. Curves need sample counts, units, intervals, or seed ranges; axes must not be cropped to show only improvement. For robots, plot trajectories, errors, constraint violations, peak force, recovery time, and failure classes together.  6.10 Configuration, command lines, and environments Research code should run from one clear command. Keep tunable parameters in a config, allow a small number of command-line overrides, and log environment information. Do not scatter paths, seeds, and devices across global variables in many scripts; that turns maintenance or simulator changes into archaeology.  6.11 Debugging ladder: reduce the problem before restoring complexity   6.12 Maintainable boundaries for scientific code Separate code into four layers: pure functions, data layer, algorithm layer, and adapters for ROS, simulators, or hardware. Pure functions are easiest to test; adapters are most version-sensitive. When a new resource arrives, update the adapter or configuration rather than scattering version checks through algorithms. The acceptance object of a scientific-code boundary is run identity, not a module name. Explicit seeds and configuration narrow the RMSE distribution; hidden randomness widens it even when the same algorithm is called. 6.13 From one control step to a reproducible experiment ledger The 2-D point-control experiment in Chapter 1 is the smallest scientific-programming loop: a function receives positions and a configuration, updates state with an explicit $\Delta t$, returns arrays and a termination reason, and a summary function generates paper metrics. Do not store only the final error; two runs with the same final error may mean “success by tolerance” and “near the target after timeout.”   6.14 Complete scientific-Python lab: make arrays auditable evidence This section redefines “knowing Python” as six research abilities: reject non-finite values, compute extreme probability scales stably, block geometric distance calculations under memory limits, attach a schema and physical frame to every row, summarize with quantiles rather than one mean, and freeze experimental conditions in immutable configuration. These basics directly determine whether point clouds, training loops, and multi-robot logs are trustworthy.   科学 Python 数值、几何、schema 与配置完整主源 / Complete scientific-Python numerical, geometry, schema, and configuration source Blocked nearest distance must match the fully broadcast result while reducing peak memory from $O(ND)$ to $O(BD)$; an empty candidate set must not return $\infty$ as if it were a distance. Configuration is validated at construction rather than when a control loop divides by zero; unknown override keys fail immediately so a typo cannot silently retain an old default. Tests cover correct values and invalid boundaries, separating numerical, shape, data-admission, and configuration faults. 科学 Python 完整契约测试 / Complete scientific-Python contract tests  6.15 Chapter recap and research exit Scientific programming is not about memorizing more APIs. It is about making shape, units, randomness, tests, and logs part of the model interface. Change a rotation matrix to one with determinant $-1$ and verify that tests detect a reflection; then remove the random seed and observe reproducibility. Minimum check: state the input shape, units, seed, and failure behavior of one function; add determinant and orthogonality assertions for a rotation matrix; run twice and compare raw logs rather than only final images. 建立一个最小研究仓库模板：`src/` 保存模型，`experiments/` 保存配置和运行脚本，`tests/` 保存性质测试，`results/` 保存原始数据和图表，并在 README 中记录一次完整运行。 Evidence-loop supplement: the chapter object Prerequisite: variables, units, timestamps, states, and failure taxonomies. Express the chapter object as $x_{t+1}=f(x_t,u_t)$ and declare inputs, outputs, frames, age, and task tolerance; a polished curve cannot support a research claim when these fields are missing.

title: Algebra, functions, and trigonometry: the foundation of motion geometry
text: 4.1 An equation is another form of a constraint Assembly problems often ask which condition a quantity must satisfy. A 2-D point $p=(x,y)$ on a circle of radius $r$ satisfies $x^2+y^2=r^2$. This is not an isolated algebra exercise; it is a minimal model for reachable boundaries, trajectory constraints, and collision geometry.  Writing the constraint as $g=0$ lets us check the residual $|g|$ in code. In more complex robot models, the residual becomes a metric for optimization and experiment evaluation.  4.2 A function graph visualizes a model A function graph makes the relation between input and output observable. Sine and cosine are not only exam formulas; they describe rotations, periodic motion, and joint trajectories. Plot first, then discuss amplitude, phase, and period, so symbols do not become decoration.   Changing $A$ changes the motion range, changing $\omega$ changes the speed, and changing $\phi$ changes the initial state. Every change should be explained in physical language, not merely described as “the curve changed.” 4.3 Angles, radians, and the unit circle Trigonometric functions usually take radians because the ratio of arc length to radius keeps derivative formulas simple: $\frac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta=\cos\theta$. Code libraries almost always expect radians. Mixing degrees and radians is one of the most common and subtle foundational errors in robot programs.   4.4 Inverse trigonometric functions and pose estimation When a sensor gives a direction vector $(v_x,v_y)$, use `atan2(v_y,v_x)` to obtain its heading. `atan2` handles quadrants, unlike $\arctan(v_y/v_x)$, which loses sign information and fails when $v_x=0$.  4.5 Absolute values, inequalities, and safety boundaries “Error must be below 0.2 mm” is the absolute-value inequality $|e|\le0.2$; a force limit is $F_{\min}\le F\le F_{\max}$. Absolute value folds direction into magnitude, useful for safety and anomaly detection, but signed error must also be kept when direction has physical meaning.  4.6 Exponentials, logarithms, and scale changes Exponentials and logarithms appear in probability, losses, sensor dynamic range, and time constants. $e^x$ maps additive scale to multiplicative scale; $\log$ maps products to sums. In optimization, log-likelihood is more stable than multiplying probabilities. Contact force, image brightness, and rewards can span orders of magnitude, so ask about scale before choosing a function.   4.7 Trigonometric identities and coordinate projection The identity $\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta$ explains why serial-joint angles add: the second link direction rotates by $\beta$ relative to the first. Projection formulas $v_x=\|v\|\cos\theta,\ v_y=\|v\|\sin\theta$ convert polar to Cartesian coordinates. Draw the vector before writing the identity.  4.8 Phase, frequency, and sampling of periodic functions The period of $q(t)=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$ is $T=2\pi/\omega$. Sampling too slowly creates aliasing: a fast motion may appear slow and become impossible to identify. Configure sampling from the highest frequency of interest and log both raw rate and resampling method.  4.9 Scaling analysis: does the equation make physical sense Dimensional analysis is the cheapest error check. Position error cannot be added directly to angle error; combine them only through a radius, a Jacobian, or an explicit weight. Torque is N m, power is N m/s, and probability is dimensionless. Put units in variable names and plot axes to bridge formulas and code.   4.10 Complete algebra and trigonometry lab: from symbols to robot trajectories This lab does not append unrelated NumPy functions. It connects five mathematical threads into one causal chain: intervals represent constraints, stable functions handle extreme scales, polar coordinates represent planar direction, sinusoids generate continuous trajectories, and dimensionless error combines task metrics with different units. Every function declares its domain before computing; invalid domains fail at the mathematical boundary rather than becoming NaN, a wrong quadrant, or an unsafe action inside the controller.   代数、三角、轨迹和无量纲误差完整主源 / Complete algebra, trigonometry, trajectory, and dimensionless-error source The tests require more than returning a number. Polar round trips freeze quadrant semantics; analytic-versus-finite-difference velocity freezes derivative semantics; softplus at $x=\pm1000$ freezes numerical stability; and zero direction, NaN, and zero tolerance deliberately construct counterexamples. A round-trip failure localizes to angle and quadrant, a derivative failure to time and scale, an extreme-value failure to the numerical formula, and an unreported invalid input to interface admission. 代数与三角完整契约测试 / Complete algebra-and-trigonometry contract tests  4.11 Chapter recap and research exit This chapter treated equations as constraints, functions as input-output models, and trigonometric functions as the language of rotation and periodic motion. Finish by plotting $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, comparing `atan` with `atan2`, and connecting periodic joint trajectories to 2R forward kinematics. Explain how parameters determine range, speed, and period. Minimum check: convert an angle between degrees and radians and verify the round-trip error; compare `atan` and `atan2` on the same direction vector; then describe in words how a periodic joint trajectory will enter 2R forward kinematics, without computing matrices now. 留下两份证据：一张标注弧度和象限的图，以及一段能检查角度单位的测试代码。 Evidence-loop supplement: the chapter object Prerequisite: variables, units, timestamps, states, and failure taxonomies. Express the chapter object as $x_{t+1}=f(x_t,u_t)$ and declare inputs, outputs, frames, age, and task tolerance; a polished curve cannot support a research claim when these fields are missing.

title: Vectors, matrices, and frames: when mathematics becomes a robot action
text: 矩阵作为带输入输出语义的映射：普通变换与近奇异变换 / A matrix as a typed map: regular and near-singular actions 2.0 Where matrices come from: collecting many operations into one action Do not begin by treating a matrix as a table of numbers. Suppose an assembly table maps $(x,y)$ to two outputs. If the rules are $u=2x-y$ and $v=x+3y$, collect the coefficients according to which output depends on which input.     A matrix is not an arbitrary notation: it compresses a collection of linear equations into a reusable input-output interface. A $2\times2$ matrix means two inputs and two outputs. If the input has three entries while the output still has two, the matrix naturally becomes $2\times3$.  2.1 Start from the task: turning a camera point into a robot action Suppose a camera observes a datum hole on an aero-engine blade. The vision module returns image coordinates $(u,v)$, a depth module reconstructs a point $p^C$ in the camera frame, and the controller needs the same point $p^B$ in the robot-base frame. For a camera fixed on the workbench, the minimal computational chain is  The equation is short, but it hides four engineering questions. Are the coordinates in metres or millimetres? Does the subscript $BC$ mean “express $C$ in $B$” under our convention? Should a point and a free direction vector use the same transform? How large can calibration error be before the assembly clearance is exhausted? Each hidden question becomes an explicit interface or check in this chapter.  2.2 A vector is not merely a column of numbers: semantics, units, and frames first A vector is first a semantic object and only then a sequence of numbers. A position says where a point is, a displacement says how one position changes to another, a velocity says how position changes over time, and an error says how the current state differs from a target. They may all have three entries, but equal shapes do not make them interchangeable.  The superscript $B$ denotes a coordinate frame; subscripts can denote an object or a time role. A reliable engineering record must answer what an array represents, in which frame, in which unit, and at which timestamp. Such metadata are often omitted on paper; in a real robot, that omission is a source of failure.  An immediate check When you see `error = goal - current`, do not first ask whether NumPy can execute it. Ask whether the arrays represent the same kind of object, share a frame, share a unit, and refer to compatible times. Only four “yes” answers make the subtraction physically meaningful. 2.3 Matrix order: a contract between input and output spaces Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be an $n$-dimensional column vector and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ an $m$-dimensional output. A matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ represents a linear map from the input space to the output space: $y=Ax$. Thus, $m$ rows and $n$ columns are not formatting facts; they state how many input components the action consumes and how many output components it produces.  From the row view, each row is a linear measurement of the input. From the column view, column $j$ is the image of the input basis vector $e_j$. Therefore  The columns tell us what happens to the basis directions of the input space. For a rotation matrix, columns are the rotated coordinate axes; for a camera projection, they describe image changes caused by 3-D directions. The later Jacobian will reuse this interpretation, but this chapter does not require computing one yet.  2.4 Why matrix multiplication has an order: composition of actions If action $A$ first maps an input to an intermediate object $z$ and action $B$ maps $z$ to the output $y$, then  The rightmost matrix acts first because this is function composition. If a point goes from the tool frame $E$ to the wrist frame $W$ and then to the base frame $B$, the chain is  Swapping two matrices often does not trigger a shape error because the dimensions remain compatible, but it changes the physical action. The following planar example deliberately separates “translate then rotate” from “rotate then translate.”   Both results look like reasonable coordinates, but they describe different actions. In research code, a transform chain should be expressed by frame labels and tests rather than by the author's memory. 2.5 Rotation matrices: preserving length and angle, not arbitrary 2-D matrices A 2-D rotation matrix is determined by one angle:  It satisfies $R^TR=I$ and $\det R=1$. The first identity says the columns are orthonormal; the second excludes a mirror reflection. Therefore  This derivation explains why rotation does not change the distance between two points on a rigid body. It also gives a code assertion: if a purported rotation changes lengths noticeably, first check angle units, numeric types, and frame indices before tuning a controller.  2.6 Frames: several numerical expressions of one physical point A physical point has one location, but its numerical expression can differ across frames. A camera observes $p^C$, the robot base uses $p^B$, and a world model uses $p^W$. Frame labels must be explicit; otherwise subtraction, interpolation, and control errors have no precise meaning. 一个物理点的多 frame 表达，以及 frame 误差如何消耗装配间隙 / One physical point in multiple frames, and how frame error consumes assembly clearance Do not casually mix active rotation of an object with passive change of coordinates. A project may choose either convention, but it must fix the convention and state input and output frames in every API.  2.7 Homogeneous transforms: why append a 1 Rotation is written as $Rp$ and translation as $p+t$. With only a $2\times2$ matrix, translation cannot be composed by the same multiplication. Homogeneous coordinates augment a planar point to $\tilde p=[p^T,1]^T$:  Expanding the last row shows that the homogeneous component remains one; expanding the first two rows gives $p^B=R_{BA}p^A+t_{BA}$. The extra dimension does not add a physical degree of freedom. It embeds an affine action in a composable linear representation.  The difference between a point and a direction vector is explicit in homogeneous coordinates: a point has last component 1, while a free vector has last component 0. The same $T$ therefore translates a point but not a direction.  2.8 Transform chains: use subscripts as a type system Use the convention that $T_{BA}$ converts an expression in frame $A$ into an expression in frame $B$. Then  This is analogous to function types or unit checking: a chain is legal only when the output frame of one transform equals the input frame of the next. Bare matrices allow many dimensionally valid but physically wrong products; frame-aware objects can reject them early.  Paper diagnosis: trace one point along the arrows  2.9 Runnable lab I: a FrameTransform that fails loudly The class below stores four pieces of metadata together: source frame, target frame, length unit, and matrix. It is not object-oriented ornamentation; it turns a physical constraint that would otherwise live only in comments into an executable check.  Inspect the interface before inspecting the numbers. The last homogeneous component is 1 for `apply_point` and effectively 0 for `apply_vector`; `then` allows $A\to B$ only to be followed by $B\to C$. These design choices determine whether later numerical results deserve trust.  If a free direction is incorrectly passed as a point, the result is $[2,4]^T$ instead of $[0,1]^T$. This can simultaneously corrupt end-effector orientation, contact normals, and force-control directions without raising an exception. 2.10 Runnable lab II: planar calibration from corresponding rigid points We now move from a known matrix action to an action estimated from data. Camera-to-base extrinsics can be estimated from corresponding points. Given camera points $p_i^C$ and base points $p_i^B$, we seek  Translation and rotation are coupled in the original expression. Subtracting the two centroids removes translation:    Let $H=(Q^C)^TQ^B$ and compute its SVD $H=U\Sigma V^T$. The 2-D Kabsch solution is $R=VDU^T$, with the last singular direction negated if the unconstrained solution is a reflection. This estimates a matrix while preserving the rigid-body constraint instead of fitting unconstrained entries.  The smallest singular value also supports degeneracy detection. If all calibration points nearly coincide, or their geometry is insufficient to determine rotation, the SVD tells us that the problem is unidentifiable instead of returning a seemingly precise pose. 2.11 Error, noise, and conditioning: why point layout matters Even without obvious outliers, a point set may be unable to estimate rotation stably. If points are tightly clustered, small pixel or depth noise can cause a large angular change; if they are nearly collinear, information in some directions is missing. Numerical linear algebra describes this as ill-conditioning or a large condition number.  Here $\kappa$ is not an abstract score of algorithm quality; it warns how the data geometry amplifies error. A calibration experiment should report point-set scale, spatial coverage, the smallest singular value, fit RMSE, and repetitions across noise levels and seeds rather than one attractive matrix.  2.12 Shapes, units, and assertions in code A NumPy array knows its shape and dtype, but not metres, base frame, or whether it is a direction. The minimum coding standard in this book is therefore not “it runs” but “errors become visible early.”  For example, `np.matmul` can multiply a $(3,3)$ matrix by a $(3,)$ array, but it cannot tell whether that array is a point or a vector, nor which way the matrix maps frames. A good interface preserves semantics before and after the call; a good experiment gives a diagnostic message when an assertion fails. 2.13 Full experiment: from ground truth and noise to a reproducible report Running `linear_algebra_frames_lab.py` produces four metrics: fit RMSE, the ground-truth RMSE on noisy data, translation error, and rotation error. A fixed seed makes the run reproducible; it does not make one seed sufficient evidence for a method.   In research, changing one variable at a time is more valuable than running arbitrary extra trials. First fix the point set and ground truth and sweep noise; then fix noise and compare clustered points with points covering the workspace. This separates algorithmic error from observation geometry. 2.13A Complete source and contract tests: matrices must carry frame semantics The hand calculations and snippets above explain how a matrix acts. The complete module below explains how software rejects physically meaningless but dimensionally legal multiplication. `FrameTransform` stores source, target, unit, and a homogeneous matrix. Points use homogeneous coordinate 1, vectors use only the rotation block, composition requires matching intermediate frames and units, and inversion swaps semantic direction. A bare matrix lacks this information and should remain an internal implementation rather than a system interface.  frame、齐次变换、SVD 刚体拟合与标定报告完整主源 / Complete frame, homogeneous-transform, SVD rigid-fit, and calibration-report source Tests first distinguish translation semantics for points and vectors, then check frame composition and unit mismatch. They recover a ground-truth transform from noiseless correspondences, perform an inverse round trip, inject a NaN angle, a non-orthogonal rotation, collinear calibration points, and empty RMSE data, and finally verify exact report reproducibility under a fixed seed. If foundational geometry fails, PnP, hand--eye calibration, visual servoing, and multi-robot state fusion must not continue. 线性代数与 frame 完整契约测试 / Complete linear-algebra and frame contract tests  2.14 Failure cases: why a plausible result can still be wrong Failure 1: mixing degrees and radians Python trigonometric functions use radians. If $90$ is passed as radians, $\cos(90)$ is about $-0.448$, not 0. The matrix remains $2\times2$ and the program runs; only invariants or visualization

title: Functions, derivatives, and Jacobians: how change propagates
text: 有限差分步长、雅可比检验与奇异位形 / Finite-difference scale, Jacobian audit, and a singular pose 3.1 A function: a derivative needs inputs, outputs, and units A function $y=f(x)$ maps an object from an input space to an output space. Forward kinematics is a function: joint angles $q$ pass through the mechanism to produce end-effector position $p$. Without the input, output, frame, and units of a function, its derivative has no object to describe.  Thus $\partial p/\partial q$ has units m/rad; it is not a unitless matrix. Unit analysis prevents errors in control gains, normalization, and simulation interfaces. Treating an m/rad Jacobian as m/deg changes the scale by $180/\pi$.  3.2 One-variable derivatives: local slope and prediction For a scalar function, the derivative describes the local slope:  The engineering prediction is the first-order approximation:  For $f(x)=x^2+2x$ at $x=1.5$, $f'(1.5)=5$. An input increase of $0.01$ predicts an output increase of about $0.05$; the second-order term determines the error. State this prediction before writing the limit definition.  With a large $h$, neglected higher-order terms cause truncation error. With a small $h$, subtracting nearly equal function values amplifies floating-point roundoff. The error usually decreases and then rises. This balance between approximation and numerical error returns in finite-difference Jacobians, gradient checks, and simulation integration. 3.3 Multivariable functions: partial, directional, and Jacobian derivatives When both input and output are vectors, the derivative is a linear map rather than a scalar. For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, near $x$  Column $j$ is the output change caused by moving along input basis direction $e_j$; row $i$ describes the sensitivity of output $i$ to all input components. This is exactly the matrix interpretation from Chapter 2.  is the directional derivative along $v$. It answers “what instantaneous end-effector velocity results from joint velocity $v$?” rather than “what happens when one variable changes in isolation.” 3.4 A 2R arm: deriving forward kinematics from geometry Consider a planar two-revolute-joint arm with link lengths $l_1,l_2$ and joint angles $q_1,q_2$. The absolute direction of the second link is $q_1+q_2$, so the end position is the sum of two vectors:  Do not memorize this as a standard answer. Draw the two links, project each onto $x$ and $y$, and add them. Different joint conventions may change signs, but the geometric reasoning remains.  3.5 Deriving the Jacobian: each column is one joint's local effect Differentiate $p(q)$ with respect to $q_1$ and $q_2$:  The first column contains both links because $q_1$ rotates both; the second contains only the second link because $q_2$ changes only the relative angle. This physical interpretation matters more than copying the formula into a matrix.   3.6 The chain rule: from local coordinates to complex models Robotic systems are compositions: a sensor maps state to features, a policy maps features to actions, and a controller maps actions to joint commands. If $z=g(x)$ and $y=f(z)$, then  This explains two things. First, backpropagation is the chain rule organized on a computation graph, not a new kind of magic. Second, robot transform and Jacobian chains must match intermediate spaces; multiplying a Jacobian in one frame by a velocity in another is a malformed chain rule. 3.7 Verify the Jacobian with finite differences: test the approximation The analytic derivation gives  A verification should track three things: whether the step is small enough, whether the error decreases with the step, and whether numerical sensitivity appears near singular configurations. Comparing one output array only proves that one call did not crash.   3.8 Singularity and conditioning: which task directions are difficult When the columns of $J$ become nearly linearly dependent, the two joint effects point in nearly the same direction and some end-effector motions become difficult. For the planar 2R arm,  Thus the arm is singular when $q_2=0$ or $\pi$, where it is straight or folded. Numerically, singular values $\sigma_{\max},\sigma_{\min}$ and the condition number $\kappa=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$ are more robust indicators. They can be monitored as controller safety signals.  3.9 Inverse differential kinematics: from task velocity to joint velocity To achieve a task velocity $v$, the ideal relation is $J\dot q=v$. If $J$ is invertible, $\dot q=J^{-1}v$; more generally use the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $J^\dagger$:  Near a singularity use a damped pseudoinverse:  Damping introduces bias but limits velocity amplification. A larger $\lambda$ is not always safer because it reduces task tracking accuracy. Schedule it from singular values, joint speed limits, and task tolerance.  3.10 Turn the rate map into a control experiment: discrete time and safety A rate-level controller is not yet a complete control system. A discrete implementation needs a sampling period $\Delta t$:  A minimal point controller sets $e=p_{goal}-p(q)$, requests $v=Ke$, and maps it through the damped pseudoinverse. It must additionally check joint limits, speed clipping, collisions, and singularity.  Failure in this experiment does not mean the Jacobian method is invalid. Record whether failure came from an unreachable target, a singular start, speed clipping, joint limits, or a large time step. A research report should separate these causes. 3.11 Automatic differentiation and gradient checks: a shared language Automatic differentiation obtains derivatives from a computation graph using the chain rule; it is not symbolic differentiation and is not finite differences. Finite differences remain valuable as an independent numerical sanity check. For a new loss or Jacobian, compare autodiff and finite differences on small fixed inputs before training or control.  If autodiff disagrees with the analytic expression, first check tensor shapes, broadcasting, angle units, accidental detachment, and whether the loss is the intended physical quantity. “It backpropagates” does not mean “the gradient is correct.” 3.12 Failure cases: a correct derivative can still fail   3.13 Exercises and answer skeletons   3.14 Bilingual terminology and interview practice   3.15 Cross-Part linearization evidence: do not merely trust $J\delta q$ At this point, a derivative or Jacobian should not remain a formula that can merely be written down. It is a local model: near the current $q$, $J(q)\delta q$ predicts the actual endpoint displacement. Research use asks one more question: for which step sizes, postures, and task directions is that local model trustworthy? This section turns the Taylor remainder into measurable evidence rather than an abstract higher-order term.   For smooth forward kinematics and a non-degenerate direction, the absolute remainder is usually $O(h^2)$ and the relative error is usually $O(h)$. This is not a promise that every implementation must produce slope one: near singular postures, angle branches, clipping, or noise can change the slope. Report the observed slope, endpoint residual (m), step (rad), and $\sigma_{\min}(J)$ (m/rad), together with the validity range.      3.16 Completion standard and research exit Minimum evidence: hand-derive one term of 2R forward kinematics; explain each Jacobian column; run the analytic/finite-difference comparison; run `test_linearization_evidence_lab.py` and report the observed relative-error order; run a damped pseudoinverse near a singular pose; record one controller failure cause; and explain Jacobians, units, and singularities in Chinese and English. Connect the frame-aware transform from Chapter 2 to this Jacobian in a 2R point-reaching experiment. Record the target, trajectory, end-effector error, peak joint speed, smallest singular value, and failure cause across targets, postures, noise, and control periods.

title: Probability and statistics: making uncertainty measurable
text: 重复观测与区间宽度：不确定性进入观测合同 / Repeated observations and interval width: uncertainty enters the observation contract 5.1 A random variable is not just a random number A random variable maps an uncertain outcome to a number. When repeatedly observing the same blade tip, $Z$ can denote the measured depth. Its distribution describes the structure of possible outcomes; one measurement is only one sample from that distribution.  The mean describes the center and the variance describes spread. Neither is accuracy by itself: a sensor can be stable but biased, or unbiased on average but highly variable. Bias and variance must be examined together. 5.2 Estimate mean and variance with repeated experiments  A fixed random seed supports reproducibility; it does not pretend that the world is deterministic. Real experiments still need sensor, environment, sampling-rate, and outlier records. The seed only gives debugging and comparison a common starting point. 5.3 Histograms, density, and outliers Plot data before choosing a distribution. A histogram can reveal symmetry, multiple modes, and outliers. Do not assume a Gaussian distribution immediately; distributional assumptions affect filtering, confidence intervals, and safety margins.  Random noise can often be reduced by repeated measurements and averaging. Systematic bias does not disappear automatically with more samples. Wrong camera extrinsics, unit mistakes, or occlusion require recalibration, a changed model, or a changed experiment. 5.4 Conditional probability and Bayesian updating When a robot has both a model prediction and a sensor measurement, the central question is how plausible a state is given existing information. Bayes' rule connects prior, likelihood, and posterior:  We do not jump to the Kalman filter yet. First identify the roles: $p(x)$ is the belief before the measurement, $p(z\mid x)$ is the likelihood of observing $z$ if the state were $x$, and $p(x\mid z)$ is the updated belief after seeing $z$. These roles return in state estimation. 5.5 Confidence intervals and experimental language “The mean error is 2 mm” is not enough. Report sample count, statistic, distributional assumptions, and how the interval was obtained. Research figures should show variability rather than only the most attractive mean. 5.6 Covariance: how multiple errors vary together Position/orientation errors, or two end-effector errors relative to a part, are usually not independent. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the covariance is  The diagonal contains variances; off-diagonal entries show coupled errors. Elliptical confidence regions come from eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $\Sigma$. Ignoring correlations turns a tilted error cloud into an axis-aligned rectangle and can make safety margins too loose or too conservative.  5.7 Gaussian models, standardization, and z-scores The one-dimensional Gaussian density is  A z-score is $(z-\mu)/\sigma$. It puts measurements with different units on a common scale but does not remove bias or correlation. Estimate $\mu,\sigma$ only from training or calibration data; recomputing them on test data leaks information.  5.8 Bootstrap: resample uncertainty itself When distributional assumptions are unreliable, resample observations with replacement, compute the statistic repeatedly, and use quantiles for an empirical interval. Bootstrap does not create physical information; it expresses uncertainty from the current data and cannot replace independent tests or more part coverage.  5.9 Correlation, causality, and intervention If peak force correlates with failure rate, high force may cause failure, or small clearance may cause both high force and failure, or the controller may increase force in difficult scenes. Observational data show association; causal claims require a controllable intervention, randomized order, confounder records, and a no-intervention baseline.  5.10 Error propagation: how input uncertainty reaches actions For output $y=f(x)$, a local Jacobian propagates covariance under small perturbations:  This explains why the same pixel error produces different end-effector errors at different poses, and why conditioning and observation geometry belong in calibration. Linearization may fail under large occlusion, contact switches, or multimodal posteriors; use Monte Carlo rollouts or particle methods there.  5.11 Confidence intervals, prediction intervals, and replication A confidence interval concerns the population mean; a prediction interval concerns a future individual trial and is wider. Robotics papers should separate uncertainty across episodes, across parts, and in one action's sensor noise rather than using one standard deviation for everything.  5.12 Bayesian updating and the state-estimation interface Bayes' rule connects prior, likelihood, and posterior:  We do not jump to the Kalman filter yet. First identify the roles: $p(x)$ is the belief before the measurement, $p(z\mid x)$ is the likelihood of observing $z$ if the state were $x$, and $p(x\mid z)$ is the updated belief after seeing $z$. These roles return in state estimation. 5.13 Chapter recap and research exit The minimum outcome is to estimate mean and variance from repeated trials, plot a distribution, distinguish bias from noise, and explain prior, likelihood, and posterior. Run 20 simulated measurements with separate fixed bias and random noise, then observe what more samples can and cannot remove. Minimum check: estimate the mean, variance, and a 95% interval from measurements with fixed bias and random noise; state the roles of prior, likelihood, and posterior; and explain why more samples cannot remove fixed bias. 为叶片尖端视觉定位设计误差报告模板，至少包含均值、标准差、最大误差、95% 分位数、样本数、遮挡条件和坐标系。 5.14 Complete loop: from distributions to assembly release Prerequisite: means, variance, conditional probability, and percentiles. Write a measurement as $z=\mu+b+\epsilon$, where $b$ is fixed bias and $\epsilon$ is random noise. More samples reduce uncertainty about $\epsilon$ but do not remove $b$.

title: Optimization basics: turning “better” into a checkable objective
text: 8.1 Variables, objectives, and constraints An optimization problem has at least three layers: variables $x$ are what we choose; an objective $J(x)$ measures quality; constraints $g(x)\le0$ or $h(x)=0$ encode what cannot be violated. A discretized joint trajectory may contain $q_0,\ldots,q_N$. Its objective can penalize end-effector error, velocity changes, and energy, while constraints enforce joint limits, speed limits, and collision clearance.  “Minimize position error” is not a complete task specification. In which frame is the error measured? How are translation and rotation weighted? Is collision a hard constraint or a penalty? What threshold counts as success? These decisions define the landscape seen by the optimizer and determine whether another researcher can reproduce the result. 8.2 The gradient as a local direction For a one-dimensional function, the derivative says whether moving right increases or decreases the function. In multiple dimensions, the gradient $\nabla J(x)$ collects directional rates of change. A local approximation is  Choosing $\Delta x=-\alpha\nabla J(x)$ gives gradient descent. It tends to decrease the objective only under local conditions and a suitable step size; it does not guarantee a global optimum.   8.3 Least squares and calibration Many robotics problems can be written as making residuals small: $\min_\theta\|A\theta-b\|_2^2$. This appears in camera calibration, joint zero-offset estimation, sensor bias fitting, and simple dynamics identification. The normal equation $A^\mathsf{T}A\theta=A^\mathsf{T}b$ is useful for intuition, but engineering code usually uses QR or SVD instead of explicitly forming a potentially ill-conditioned $A^\mathsf{T}A$.  The residual norm is not the only evidence. Check whether parameters are physically meaningful, whether residuals change across the sample distribution, whether the matrix is ill-conditioned, and whether held-out samples are predicted well. A calibration model that works near one pose should not be extrapolated blindly to the whole assembly workspace. 8.4 Constraints, penalties, and projection If a variable must satisfy $l\le x\le u$, the simplest method is projection after each update: $x\leftarrow\min(\max(x,l),u)$. For more complex constraints, add violation to the objective, for example $J_{pen}=J+\lambda\max(0,g(x))^2$. Projection means “never leave the set”; a penalty means “leaving is expensive.” Both require careful scaling and weight checks.  8.5 Trajectory costs and numerical scale Trajectory optimization often combines several physical intentions:  Weights should not be tuned only until a plot looks good. Normalize terms to comparable, dimensionless ranges, then report ablations showing what happens when each term is removed. Otherwise it is impossible to tell whether an improvement came from the algorithm or from the weights.  8.6 Chapter recap and research exit Optimization is a modeling language. It decomposes “faster, safer, more accurate, and more stable” into variables, objectives, constraints, and evidence. Before learning a new algorithm, write a small problem by hand, check one gradient with finite differences, and compare constrained and unconstrained results. Then, when you meet planning, calibration, or reinforcement learning, you will know what the algorithm is actually optimizing. Minimum check: decompose “better” into variables, objectives, and constraints; check one gradient with finite differences; compare two initializations with constrained and unconstrained runs; and explain why a decreasing objective can still produce task failure. 为一个二维末端轨迹写出至少四项代价：终点位姿误差、速度平滑、与障碍物的距离和总时间。给出每项的单位、归一化方式、权重、硬约束和成功阈值，并用两个不同初值运行梯度下降，记录失败模式。 8.7 A complete problem card: from a robot goal to an auditable objective A research-grade optimization problem has at least five layers: decision variable $z$, computable state map $x=f(z)$, component costs $c_i$, hard constraints $g_j(z)\leq0$, and task acceptance metrics independent of the cost. Collapsing them into one scalar prevents you from answering whether the cost improved or the task actually improved.  8.8 Executable modeling semantics: scales, residuals, and projection `weighted_objective` requires a scale and weight for every term; a scale does not make numbers look nice, it places metres, radians, newtons, and seconds in a comparable dimensionless space. `least_squares_report` reports residual, gradient, and rank together; `project_box` returns the intervention, showing whether constraints are modifying the action. 优化问题建模完整主源 / Complete optimization-formulation source 尺度、残差、投影与放行测试 / Scale, residual, projection, and gate tests  8.9 Research exit: a fair protocol for replacing optimizers When comparing gradient descent, SQP, MPC, or reinforcement learning, fix the problem card, data, initializations, stopping budget, and acceptance metrics before changing the solver. Every method must output the same component costs, constraint violations, compute time, failure reason, and seed; otherwise “the new method is better” may only mean that the scale or denominator changed. Evidence-loop supplement: the chapter object Prerequisite: variables, units, timestamps, states, and failure taxonomies. Express the chapter object as $x_{t+1}=f(x_t,u_t)$ and declare inputs, outputs, frames, age, and task tolerance; a polished curve cannot support a research claim when these fields are missing.
